faqs.question: How do you say "I miss you" in Sanskrit?
faqs.answer: You cannot say it the way English says it, because Sanskrit has no transitive verb meaning "to miss someone." What it has is the noun विरह (viraha), which Apte's dictionary defines on page 1461 as "Parting with, separation" and "Especially, the separation of lovers." If you want one word, that is the word.

faqs.question: What does viraha actually mean?
faqs.answer: Apte, page 1461, gives separation, the separation of lovers, absence, want, desertion, the feeling of love in separation, and loneliness. Monier-Williams, page 982 column 3, files it as a masculine noun: "abandonment, desertion, parting, separation (esp. of lovers), absence from." Both dictionaries agree on the core sense, and both narrow it to lovers.

faqs.question: Is विरह safe to put on a tattoo?
faqs.answer: It is the safest of the options here: one noun, two independent lexicons, no second entry with an embarrassing gloss. One detail matters — the dictionary stem is विरह, while विरहः with the final visarga is the nominative singular. With nothing around it to govern the case, the bare stem is the safer thing to carve.

faqs.question: What is the difference between viraha and utkaṇṭhā?
faqs.answer: विरह names the state of being separated; उत्कण्ठा names the feeling of longing inside it. Apte, page 403, gives utkaṇṭhā as "Longing for a beloved person or thing" and "Regret, sorrow, missing any thing or person" — the only place in either dictionary where a lexicographer used the English word "missing" directly.

faqs.question: Why does utkaṇṭhā literally mean something about the throat?
faqs.answer: Apte brackets the etymology as उन्नतः कण्ठो यस्य, "having the neck uplifted," and Monier-Williams glosses the adjective the same way, adding "having the throat open (as in crying)." The image behind the word is a neck craned to look for someone who has not arrived yet.

faqs.question: What is vipralambha-śṛṅgāra?
faqs.answer: It is one of the two halves of the erotic sentiment in Sanskrit poetics — love-in-separation, against संभोगशृङ्गार, love-in-union. Apte, page 1452, calls it "the feeling or sentiment of love in separation" and quotes a definition making it five-fold, caused by desire, separation, jealousy, प्रवास (being away from home) and a curse.

faqs.question: Is Sanskrit written in the same script as Hindi?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and that is the problem. Devanagari is one script shared by Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi and Nepali, and the Unicode Character Database version 18.0.0 gives it a single block, U+0900 to U+097F, with no separate Sanskrit range. Nothing about the characters tells you which language you are looking at.

faqs.question: A tattoo artist sent me a design — how do I know it is not Hindi?
faqs.answer: Look each word up as a headword in Apte on the Digital Dictionaries of South Asia, searching the roman transliteration and not forcing an exact match. Then read the gloss rather than counting results: searching hai returns है, "a vocative particle," which has nothing to do with the Hindi verb, so a hit alone proves nothing.

faqs.question: Does smarāmi tvām mean "I miss you"?
faqs.answer: No. It means roughly "I remember you." Monier-Williams, page 1271, gives √smṛ as "to remember, recollect … (gen. or acc.)" and adds "to remember or think of with sorrow or regret," so the missing is a shading of remembering rather than its own verb. I did not print the composed line here because no corpus attests it.

faqs.question: Why do translation tools get Sanskrit wrong so often?
faqs.answer: Sanskrit fuses words together at the boundaries, and pulling them apart again is genuinely hard. The best published system, reported in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence on 28 July 2026, reaches 79.34% exact segmentation accuracy — and that is the easier job of splitting, not the harder job of composing a correct sentence.

faqs.question: Is there a Sanskrit word for the person doing the missing?
faqs.answer: Yes: विरहिन् (virahin), which Monier-Williams glosses "separated, parted (esp. from a beloved person), lonely, solitary," with the feminine विरहिणी, "a woman separated from her husband or lover." Read the rest of that entry before engraving it, though — both dictionaries also record विरहिणी as "wages, hire."

article.contentMarkdown:
# I Miss You in Sanskrit: What the Dictionaries Actually Support

Sanskrit has no verb meaning "to miss you." The nearest honest answer is a noun — **विरह**, *viraha* in IAST transliteration — which Apte's *Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary* defines on page 1461 as "Parting with, separation" and, in its second sense, "Especially, the separation of lovers."

Monier-Williams agrees. That is the word, and this page gives the page number rather than a screenshot.

The stakes are not a text message. Nobody sends Sanskrit to a partner who is away; people want this for a tattoo, an engraving, a wedding card or a caption, where a mistake is permanent and public.

Our own data shows the opposite instinct: of 214 "I miss you" pages built on SubhSandesh since 2026-07-28, **43.5% are password-protected** before sharing — the most private segment we have measured, against 38.5% platform-wide. One feeling, two impulses: carve it in public, or lock it behind a password.

## Sanskrit has no transitive verb for missing someone

English packs the idea into one transitive verb: *I* miss *you*. Sanskrit has no such verb, and reaches instead for a noun naming the state of separation, or for a verb of remembering.

That verb is √स्मृ, *smṛ*. Monier-Williams, page 1271 column 3, gives class 1 *smarati*, "to remember, recollect, call to mind, think of, be mindful of (gen. or acc.)", then adds the gloss closest to "miss": **"to remember or think of with sorrow or regret."**

You do not miss a person in Sanskrit. You remember them, and the remembering hurts.

## विरह (viraha): the word to engrave, and what it says

Apte, page 1461, विरहः *virahaḥ*: 1 "Parting with, separation." 2 "Especially, the separation of lovers." 6 "The feeling of love in separation." 7 "Loneliness."

Monier-Williams, page 982 column 3, files *vi-raha*, masculine: "abandonment, desertion, parting, separation (esp. of lovers), absence from (instr. or comp.)". Two independent lexicons, the same core sense, the "of lovers" narrowing in both.

The compounds are where it earns its reputation. **विरहानलः**, "the fire of separation." **विरहज्वरः**, "the fever or anguish of separation."

**विरहोत्कण्ठिता**, "a woman distressed by the absence of her lover or husband" — which Apte marks "one of the several classes of a Nāyikā in poetic compositions," a technical term rather than a flourish.

One caution before a tattooist sees it: the dictionary stem is *viraha*, while **विरहः**, with the final ः (visarga), is the nominative singular. With no inscription around it to govern the case, the bare stem विरह is safer to carve.

## Love-in-separation is a named category, not a mood

Apte's शृङ्गारः *śṛṅgāraḥ*, page 1566, is "the sentiment of love or sexual passion, the erotic sentiment (the first of the eight or nine sentiments in poetical compositions)" — and it splits in two: **संभोगशृङ्गार** and **विप्रलम्भशृङ्गार**, love-in-union and love-in-separation.

विप्रलम्भः *vipralambhaḥ*, page 1452, sense 6, is the other half: "(In Rhet.) The feeling or sentiment of love in separation, one of the two main kinds of शृङ्गार (opp. संभोग)."

Apte then quotes a definition making it **पञ्चविधः**, five-fold, caused by अभिलाष (desire; page 183, "longing of a lover"), विरह (separation), ईर्ष्या (jealousy), प्रवास — page 1108, "going or journeying abroad, being absent from one's home" — and शाप (a curse; Apte files शपः, page 1532).

Classical Sanskrit criticism had a named category for a person whose beloved is abroad, inside the first of the nine rasas.

## उत्कण्ठा (utkaṇṭhā): longing, with a trap inside it

Apte, page 403: **उत्कण्ठा**, 1 "Anxiety, uneasiness"; 2 "Longing for a beloved person or thing"; 3 **"Regret, sorrow, missing any thing or person."** Monier-Williams, page 175 column 3, gives "regretting or missing anything or a person." That is the only place in either dictionary where a lexicographer reached for the word *missing* directly.

Apte brackets the etymology **उन्नतः कण्ठो यस्य** — "having the neck uplifted" — and Monier-Williams glosses the adjective the same way, adding "having the throat open (as in crying)". The word is a neck craned for someone who has not arrived.

Now the trap. Under the adjective headword उत्कण्ठ, Apte records the nouns as "**A mode of sexual enjoyment**," and Monier-Williams independently gives *ut-kaṇṭha* masculine as "a kind of sexual union." It is still a legitimate word for longing; it is not one I would put on someone else's skin without saying that first.

The same problem sits next door. **विरहिणी** *virahiṇī*, Apte page 1461, is "a woman separated from her lover or husband" — and sense 2, in both dictionaries, is "**Wages, hire**." विप्रलम्भ, the rasa term above, has as its *first* sense in both "deception, deceit, disappointment."

## Why I will not print a Sanskrit sentence for your tattoo

I can verify words to a page number. I cannot verify a sentence, and nothing else on this query can either.

Dictionaries index lemmas, not inflected forms, so a headword search returns nothing for *tvām* or *smarāmi*. Corpora are the other route, and the Sanskrit corpus is thin: Tatoeba's entire Sanskrit collection held **77 sentences** on 2026-09-25, mostly Bhagavad Gītā verses, and not one contains any form of स्मृ, विरह or उत्कण्ठा. There is no attested modern sentence to copy.

Machines do not close the gap. The best published system for Sanskrit compound splitting — Irfan Ali and colleagues, *Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence*, 28 July 2026 — reports **79.34% exact segmentation accuracy**, an improvement on the previous state of the art.

That is the score for pulling a compound apart, strictly easier than composing one. Roughly one in five still comes out wrong.

What the dictionaries do print is an attested line. Under विरह sense 2, Apte quotes **सा विरहे तव दीना** — "she, wretched in separation from you." Note where "you" goes: तव, a genitive, the form Tatoeba's Gītā line uses in तव शिष्येण, translated there "by your disciple."

Sanskrit puts the missed person in the genitive, not an object slot, which is why a word-for-word rendering of "I miss you" produces something no Sanskrit reader would write.

One verified word is a defensible engraving. A sentence needs a Sanskritist, and anyone who hands you one in thirty seconds did not check it either.

## How to tell Sanskrit from Hindi sold as Sanskrit

Devanagari is one script shared by Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi and Nepali: the Unicode Character Database, version 18.0.0, gives it a single block, U+0900 to U+097F, with no separate Sanskrit range. Your font will not tell you which language you are reading.

The usual advice is to look each word up in a Sanskrit dictionary; I ran that test on 2026-09-25, and it half-works.

| Word you were handed | Apte headword search | What comes back | What it proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| *viraha* | 1 result | विरहः, p. 1461, "separation, esp. of lovers" | verified: gloss matches the claim |
| *utkaṇṭhā* | 1 result | उत्कण्ठा, p. 403, "missing any thing or person" | verified, but read the second entry too |
| *hai* (Hindi "is") | 1 result | है, p. 1765, "a vocative particle" | false pass: an unrelated homograph |
| *yad* (for Hindi याद) | 1 result | यद्, p. 1303, the relative pronoun | false pass: a different word |
| *main*, *tum* (Hindi) | no result | — | rejected, correctly |

Two things follow. Search the roman transliteration and do not force an exact match: Apte files nouns in the nominative, so exact-matching विरह returns nothing while the dictionary holds विरहः.

And a hit is not a verification — read the gloss. A lookup that can clear a Hindi word and reject a Sanskrit one in the same sitting is the best argument there is against engraving a sentence nobody sourced.

## What 214 private pages say about the opposite instinct

Nobody else publishes recipient-side behaviour, so we measured our own. Three caveats first. City, background music and "together since" are pickers with defaults, so their fill rates are not sender choices and are not given here as behaviour; the sender-chosen fields are the password, the voice note, the reunion date, the letter, the memories and the open-when letters. `viewCount` counts page views, not unique visitors — one recipient reopening a page twenty times is twenty views.

And n = 214 over two months, the template having gone live 2026-07-28, so no seasonal claim survives it.

| Field | Sender-chosen? | Across 214 pages |
|---|---|---|
| Password before sharing | yes | 43.5% (93 of 214) |
| Written memory | yes | 86.4% (185 of 214), 4.5 on average |
| Recorded voice note | yes | 13.6% (29 of 214) |
| City pair | no — a 15-city picker | 47 distinct pairs, not a sender signal |

Length is the number that speaks to this page. The median miss-you letter runs **88 words**; the longest is 1,024. A reader here wants one word, and the gap between 88 and 1 is the difference between sending this and carving it.

Recipients answer too: **1,434 hug taps** across 138 of the 214 pages, 512 on one alone, against 2,417 recorded views.

Most readers here want no template at all, and that is a reasonable place to stop. If you do want to send rather than engrave, the [page built for a partner who is away](/missyou-gf) is a poor fit for this reader: it assumes a romantic recipient and a reunion date, which 28.0% of senders set.

[The Last Piece, a photo jigsaw that reveals a letter a line at a time](/photo-puzzle), suits one line better — its final piece is deliberately not in the box, closer to *viraha* than any countdown.

Our [round-up of "I miss you" across languages](/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages) covers the spoken ones, and carries no Sanskrit line at all.

## What I cut, and why

Five things did not make it. The composed sentence **त्वां स्मरामि**: I verified स्मरामि as the first-person singular of √स्मृ and त्वाम् as the accusative of त्वद् on Wiktionary, but Monier-Williams licenses genitive *or* accusative here, no corpus attests the pair, and "I remember you" is not "I miss you."

**उत्कण्ठे** as a first-person verb — Apte attests only third-person उत्कण्ठते. **विरहिणी**, for "wages, hire." **विप्रलम्भ** alone, for "deceit."

And every line on the Pinterest and Instagram results for this query, cut unread: no author, no dictionary, no page number.

## Sources

- Apte, *The Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary*, Prasad Prakashan, 1957–1959, on the Digital Dictionaries of South Asia: [विरहः, p. 1461](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/apte_query.py?qs=viraha&searchhws=yes) · [विप्रलम्भः, p. 1452](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/apte_query.py?qs=vipralambha&searchhws=yes) · [उत्कण्ठा, p. 403](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/apte_query.py?qs=utka%E1%B9%87%E1%B9%ADh%C4%81&searchhws=yes)
- Monier-Williams, *A Sanskrit-English Dictionary*, 1899 — [√स्मृ, p. 1271](https://www.sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/MWScan/2020/web/webtc/getword.php?key=smf), Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries
- [Tatoeba, the Sanskrit collection](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/search?from=san&query=) — 77 sentences, checked 2026-09-25
- Irfan Ali et al., ["Uncertainty-aware joint modeling for Sanskrit compound splitting and segmentation"](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frai.2026.1873672/full), *Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence*, 28 July 2026

Of the 81 live 'miss' slugs, none is a classical language. Inside this batch, the thirteen finished siblings are all modern spoken languages or English tone posts. The language axis is therefore clean, and the subject axis is different too: every sibling writes for someone who will send a message, and this post writes for someone who will cut a word into metal or skin. No merge recommended.

SERP, RUN ONCE ON THE EXACT KEYWORD, 2026-09-25. There is no competitor article to analyse. The ten results were: instagram.com/popular/i-miss-you-in-sanskrit; three Pinterest pins; four English Wikipedia articles about songs and a film ('I Miss You (Toki o Koete)', 'I Miss You', 'I Am Missing You', 'Miss You (film)') — Google resolving the query as a title; one YouTube Short; and one BlogAdda post. Not one dictionary, not one grammar, not one article-format page by a named author. Phase 1's 'fetch the top 5 pages in full' could not be run as written because there are no five comparable pages, and per references/competitors.md the aggregator results were not opened. Any claim in this post about 'what competitors do' is therefore limited to what that result list itself shows.

FORMS VERIFIED AND PRINTED, each to a page: विरह / विरहः (Apte p. 1461; Monier-Williams p. 982 col. 3), विरहानलः, विरहज्वरः, विरहोत्कण्ठिता (all Apte p. 1461), विरहिन्/विरहिणी (Apte p. 1461; MW p. 982 col. 3), विप्रलम्भः (Apte p. 1452; MW p. 976 col. 1), शृङ्गारः and the pair संभोगशृङ्गार / विप्रलम्भशृङ्गार (Apte p. 1566), संभोगः (Apte p. 1649), उत्कण्ठा and उत्कण्ठ (Apte p. 403; MW p. 175 col. 3), उन्नतः कण्ठो यस्य (Apte p. 403), अभिलाष (p. 183), प्रवास (p. 1108), शप/शाप (p. 1532), √स्मृ / स्मरति (MW p. 1271 col. 3), and the quoted line सा विरहे तव दीना (Apte p. 1461). Transliteration throughout is IAST and is labelled as such in the body.

FORMS CUT, AND WHY — seven. (1) त्वां स्मरामि as a printed recommendation: स्मरामि is verified as the first-person singular of √smṛ in en.wiktionary.org's conjugation table for स्मरति and त्वाम् as the accusative singular of त्वद् on en.wiktionary.org (referenced there to Kümmel 2018), and Monier-Williams p. 1271 licenses gen. OR acc. for the verb — but no corpus attests the pair, the 'sorrow or regret' reading is a secondary sense, and 'I remember you' is not 'I miss you'. Printing it for an engraving is exactly the confidence this page argues against. (2) उत्कण्ठे as a first-person verb: Apte p. 403 attests only the third-person denominative उत्कण्ठते, which governs genitive or dative (उत्कण्ठते च युष्मत्सन्निकर्षस्य, U.6), so a first-person form would be my inflection, not the dictionary's. (3) विरहिणी as an engraving, for its sense 2 'Wages, hire' in both dictionaries. (4) विप्रलम्भ standing alone, for its first sense 'deception, deceit' in both dictionaries. (5) उत्कण्ठा recommended without a warning, given 'a mode of sexual enjoyment' at the neighbouring entry. (6) Every line reachable through the Pinterest, Instagram, YouTube and BlogAdda SERP results, cut unread — no author, no dictionary, no page number. (7) A Devanagari codepoint table, cut for the outbound-link budget after Unicode UCD 18.0.0 Blocks.txt and UnicodeData.txt were fetched and the block U+0900..U+097F and the codepoints U+0902 ANUSVARA and U+094D VIRAMA confirmed; the block range survives in prose with Unicode named but not linked.

CLAIM IN MY PROMPT I COULD NOT VERIFY AND THEREFORE DID NOT PRINT: that Kālidāsa's Meghadūta is 'an entire poem built on' viraha. Apte's विरह entry carries five quotation tags to a work abbreviated 'Me.' (8, 12, 29, 87, 89) and its उत्कण्ठा entry one more (85), and its √स्मृ citations include Me. 87 — but DSAL serves Apte's front matter and abbreviation key only as page scans (apte.pdf and .jpg files), so the expansion of 'Me.' could not be machine-verified within budget and is not asserted in the body. The vipralambha-śṛṅgāra material, which is the substance of that angle, is verified outright from Apte p. 1452 and p. 1566 and needs no attribution to a particular poem.

SOURCES NAMED IN PROSE WITHOUT A LINK, to stay inside the 3–6 outbound-link rule: the Unicode Character Database 18.0.0 (Devanagari block U+0900..U+097F), Apte pp. 1566, 1649, 1108, 183 and 1532, and Monier-Williams pp. 982, 976 and 175. All were fetched this session. Each is stated with its page or block reference so a reader can check it in one search. Also fetched, verified and not used: Samarth P. and Mahalingam, 'The Gemma Sutras: Fine-Tuning Gemma 3 for Sanskrit Sandhi Splitting', Proceedings of the 9th Widening NLP Workshop, ACL, Nov 2025, pp. 235–241 — it corroborates the Frontiers finding and was dropped because the source count was full, not because it is weak.

FIRST-PARTY LIMIT SPECIFIC TO THIS POST: the 214-page miss-you segment measures people sending a romantic page to a partner. The reader of this page is more likely choosing a word for a tattoo, an engraving or an invitation, and is not in that sample at all. The numbers are used here as a contrast — the private instinct against the permanent one — and not as evidence about what Sanskrit-curious readers do. The three mandatory caveats (pickers with defaults; viewCount as page views not unique visitors; n = 214 over two months from 2026-07-28, no seasonal claim) are all in body prose in the '214 private pages' section.

CATEGORY CAVEAT: categorySlug is miss-you-across-miles, matching the twelve language siblings in this batch so the cluster's internal linking holds. It half-misdescribes this readership — a person choosing a tattoo word is not separated by miles. family-and-continuity and modern-romance fit no better, and splitting one language spoke out of the cluster costs more than the mismatch does.

SOURCE CAPS AT THE MOMENT OF WRITING: capcheck.mjs re-run immediately before saving. dsal.uchicago.edu and tatoeba.org are cap-exempt reference instruments and were both fetched, not assumed. sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de and frontiersin.org were each unused elsewhere in this batch. europepmc.org/pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and diksiyonaryo.ph are at the 3-post cap and are not cited here; doi.org is not used at all, publisher URLs being used instead.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has no article-format competitor to prefer on this query — the SERP is three Pinterest pins, an Instagram aggregator, a YouTube Short, four Wikipedia song pages and one blog — so the bar is simply to be the first page that cites something checkable, and this one gives a dictionary page number for every Sanskrit form it prints, names the homograph traps in उत्कण्ठा, विरहिणी and विप्रलम्भ that a tattoo reader most needs, and is the only page anywhere on this query that says out loud why it will not hand over a sentence. What it cannot do is beat a domain-authority gap it never had to face here, and the honest weakness is that the refusal to print a composed line will lose some readers to any page that confidently prints one; if a Sanskritist ever reviews a line for us, that section should be rewritten to print it with the review named.
